chalkboard.title: How old next year?
code: print("Next year you will be " + next_year)

steps.say: The learner types 15. input always gives back text, so age is the string '15'.
age + 1 tries to add text and a number. Python refuses.
steps.error_label: TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

steps.say: Fix: convert first with age = int(input("Age: ")). Now age is 15 and next_year is 16.
Joining text needs text on both sides, so this line needs str(next_year).

pages.title: Every value has a type
paragraphs: Every value in Python has a type. 15 is an int, 1.5 is a float, '15' is a str (text), and True is a bool.
The type decides what you can do with a value. You can add two numbers or join two strings, but not add a string to a number.

key_term.definition: the kind of value (int, float, str, bool); it decides which operations are allowed.

pages.title: input() always gives text
paragraphs: Whatever the user types, input gives it back as a string, even if it looks like a number.
Convert it before you do arithmetic with int() or float(), and convert numbers back with str() before you join them to text.

key_term.definition: making a new value of another type, such as int('15') or str(15).

transcript: Every value in Python has a type, like int for whole numbers and str for text.
The type decides what you are allowed to do with the value.
You can add numbers, and you can join text, but you cannot add text to a number.
input always gives you text, even when the user types digits.
So convert with int before doing arithmetic.
And convert back with str before joining a number onto a sentence.
